title: A NEW CULTURE
author: ELIO VITTORINI (Translation of Adrián Salcedo)
subtitle: First editorial of the cultural magazine "Il Politecnico", a publication founded in Italy right after the Second World War.
content:
(September 29, 1945). No longer a culture that consoles in suffering, but a culture that protects from suffering, that fights it and eliminates it.

For a while, it will be difficult to say whether anyone or anything has won in this war. But certainly, there is much that has lost, and it is evident how it has lost. The dead, if we count them, are more children than soldiers; the rubble is of cities that had twenty-five centuries of life; of houses and libraries, of monuments, of cathedrals, of all the forms through which the civil progress of man has passed; and the fields where most blood has been shed are called Mauthausen, Majdanek, Buchenwald, Dachau.

Whose is the most serious defeat in all that has happened? There certainly was something that, through the centuries, had taught us to consider the existence of children sacred. It had also taught us that every civil achievement of man was sacred; the same for bread; the same for work. And if now millions of children have been killed, if so much that was sacred has nevertheless been struck and destroyed, the defeat is above all that of this "thing" that taught us their inviolability. Is it not above all that of this "thing" that taught us their inviolability?

This "thing", I want to say it immediately, is nothing other than culture: it which has been Greek thought, Hellenism, Romanism, Latin Christianity, medieval Christianity, humanism, the Reformation, the Enlightenment, liberalism, etc., and which today clusters around the names of Thomas Mann and Benedetto Croce, Benda, Huizinga, Dewey, Maritain, Bernanos and Unamuno, Lin Yutang and Santayana, Valéry, Gide and Berdyaev.

There is no crime committed by fascism that this culture had not already long since taught us to condemn. And if fascism has had the opportunity to commit all the crimes that this culture had already long since taught us to condemn, must we not ask this very culture how and why fascism was able to commit them?

I doubt that a champion of this culture, to which we also belong, can give us an answer different from the one we can give ourselves: and not acknowledge with us that the teaching of this culture has had only scant, perhaps no, civil influence on men.

Yet, we repeat, there is Plato in this culture. And there is Christ. I say: there is Christ. Has Jesus Christ had only scant influence? Quite the opposite. He has had a great deal. But it has been his influence, and that of all culture until today, which has generated changes almost only in the intellect of men, which has generated and thus regenerated itself, and never, or almost never, regenerated, within the possibilities of also making man. Greek thought, Latin thought, Christian thought of every age, seem to have given men only the way to disguise and justify, or even to make technical, the barbarity of their deeds. Is it a natural quality of culture to be unable to influence the deeds of men?

I deny it. If almost never (except in isolated periods and today in the U.S.S.R.) has culture been able to influence the deeds of men, it depends only on the way in which culture has manifested itself. It has preached, it has taught, it has elaborated principles and values, it has discovered continents and built machines, but it has not identified itself with society, it has not governed with society, it has not led armies for society. From what does culture draw the motive to elaborate its principles and its values? From the spectacle of what man suffers in society. Man has suffered in society, man suffers. And what does culture do for the man who suffers? It tries to console him.

Because of this way of being a consoler in which it has manifested itself until today, culture could not prevent the horrors of fascism. No social force was "its" in Italy or in Germany to prevent the advent of fascism to power, nor were the cannons, the airplanes, the tanks "its" that could have prevented the Ethiopian adventure, the fascist intervention in Spain, the "Anschluss" or the Munich Pact. But whose fault is it, if not its own, that social forces are not forces of culture, and cannons, airplanes, tanks are not "its"?

Society is not culture because culture is not society. And culture is not society because it has within itself the eternal renunciation of "rendering unto Caesar" and because its principles are only consolatory, because they are not timely renewing and effectively current, living with society itself as society itself lives. Will we ever be able to have a culture that knows how to protect man from suffering instead of limiting itself to consoling him? A culture that prevents them, that wards them off, that helps to eliminate exploitation and slavery, and to overcome need, this is the culture into which all the old culture must be transformed.

Italian culture has been particularly tested in its illusions. There is perhaps no one in Italy who is unaware of what the mortification of impotence or an abstract fury means. Will we continue, despite this, to follow the road that the Thomas Manns and the Benedetto Croces still indicate to us today? I address myself to all Italian intellectuals who have known fascism. Not only to the Marxists, but also to the idealists, also to the Catholics, also to the mystics. Are there reasons of idealism or Catholicism that oppose the transformation of culture into a culture capable of fighting against hunger and suffering?

Dealing with bread and work is still dealing with the "soul." While not wanting to deal with anything but the "soul," leaving "Caesar" to deal with bread and work as he sees fit, is to limit oneself to having an intellectual function and to give "Caesar" (or Donegani, Pirelli, Valletta) the opportunity to have a function of dominion "over the soul" of man. Can the attempt to bring about a new culture that is for the defense and no longer for the consolation of man, interest the idealists and the Catholics less than it interests us?

title: A CALL FOR A POINT ZERO
author: EDITOR
subtitle: Art, productive forces and the urgency of a new Avant-Garde.
content:
The incessant development of productive forces has once again highlighted the social character of art.

Productive forces encompass both the means of production and labor power within the same category. The former refers to tools, machinery, factory organization, and labor technology in general; the latter includes not only human energy but also technical knowledge, skills, and accumulated experience.

And what is the history of art but the history of technological development, the refinement of skill, and the consolidation of experience?

In every epoch of human history, productive forces have been unleashed by the establishment of new relations of production between existing social classes. Each region of the world has done so through its own institutions, laws, and customs, but always with its elevated classes positioned above others. Art, as a special property of productive development, has played a fundamental role in the rise, stagnation, and fall of these relations.

However, the establishment and consolidation of capitalist productive relations marked a turning point in human history. Since then, the appropriation of the means of production has become increasingly private, while the act of producing has become increasingly social, as the economic regime gathers more and more workers into the same production chains. This same shift became evident in art with the rise of the avant-gardes, whose very nature was collective and coordinated artistic production. It is also clear in their legacy, as the same contradiction operating at the productive level also applies to the artistic one: originality is no longer possible under individuality, just as production is not.

During the past century, alongside the historical possibility for human beings to reappropriate themselves—leaving behind an old order based on internal class divisions—there also appeared the potential for culture to once again become a truly integrating part of their existence. Nevertheless, despite a great collective effort, productive forces were not yet developed enough to achieve this goal within the artistic realm.

This is why, currently, the emergence of the internet and its derived devices has marked a watershed moment culturally. Cybernetic networks are not just another phenomenon; they are themselves a qualitatively distinct element in productive development. The social machinery of the internet—currently understood as a mere communication channel—is the cultural arm that the human body of the future was missing, because through it, the collective creation of new images could become a reality.

What is currently used by individualistic artists as an iron clad system in favor of the bourgeoisie becomes, in the hands of the workers, a further step in the very direction taken by the avant-garde. It is from this vantage point that a new point zero emerges: the urgent need for a new avant-garde that studies the accumulated experience of its predecessors and, within that analysis, applies its new coordinates.
